Culpable

/KUHL-puh-buhl/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Culpable means deserving blame for a wrongdoing, whether in a courtroom or in everyday life

Culpable means deserving blame for a wrongdoing, whether in a courtroom or in everyday life. The inquiry found the factory culpable for the equipment failure because required safety inspections had been skipped for months.

Worked Example

After the bikes were stolen from the garage, Priya admitted she was culpable, since she had left the door unlocked overnight.

No court is involved here — this is an everyday, moral use of the word. Priya's carelessness helped the wrong happen, so she deserves a share of the blame, which is exactly what culpable describes.

How Culpable Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

blameworthy

blameworthy: deserving to be blamed

at fault

at fault: being the one who caused the wrong

liable

liable: legally answerable for harm or loss

Antonyms

blameless

blameless: deserving no blame at all

innocent

innocent: not guilty of the wrongdoing

How Strong Is It? — careless → culpable → guilty

careless vs. culpable

careless vs. culpable: Careless is weaker than culpable — it points to sloppiness without saying anyone deserves blame or punishment for a wrong.

guilty vs. culpable

guilty vs. culpable: Guilty is stronger than culpable — it declares that the wrongdoing has been formally established, as when a court convicts someone.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — culp

Root — culp: blame, fault (Latin culpa)

Suffix — -able

Suffix — -able: deserving of, able to be

Put it together

Put it together: Latin culpa ('blame, fault') plus -able ('deserving of') builds the word's meaning transparently: culpable is literally 'deserving blame.'

Use the root in a new word: exculpate

Use the root in a new word: exculpate: The security footage helped exculpate the night janitor, lifting every trace of blame from him.

Root Check

Word Choice

Formal

Culpable works in legal settings ('culpable negligence') and in ordinary moral ones — a company, a committee, or a forgetful roommate can all be culpable. It usually takes 'for' ('culpable for the failure'). Don't confuse it with the sound-alike capable, which means able to do something and carries no blame at all.
